newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-British factory gate prices creep up in July.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-British factory gate prices creep up in July.

text.p: Prices of goods leaving British factory gates crept up in July as tax rises from the Labour government's first budget hit home but raw material costs fell sharply, thanks to the strong pound, official figures showed on Monday.

The Office for National Statistics said factory gate or output prices rose 0.2 percent in July, reversing a 0.2 percent fall in June. Prices were running 1.4 percent higher compared with a year earlier.
Economists, who had forecast a smaller increase in factory gate prices, said the rise was largely due to the July 2 budget.

"The surprise rise in headline output prices inflation was largely due to an increase in excise duties, the full effect of which was underestimated," said Geoffrey Dicks, UK economist at NatWest Markets.

But the Office for National Statistics (ONS) said the rise in factory gate prices should have been higher and only intense competition between manufacturers prevented them from passing on the full increase in duties to customers.
Chancellor of the Exchequer Gordon Brown increased the duty on petrol-based products by around three percent in his first budget.
"The increase in excise duties should have added about 0.4 percent onto output prices in July," the ONS said.
Another sharp fall in the costs of raw materials -- a direct result of the pound's relentless rally -- means factory gate prices could ease again in the months ahead.
Input prices dropped by a seasonally adjusted 0.4 percent in July and firms' costs were 9.0 percent lower in July this year compared with last.

"The strength of sterling is killing input prices at the moment, while the strength of domestic demand is allowing output prices to creep up," said Robin Marshall, chief economist at Chase Investment Bank.
The pound slid against the mark after the Bank of England raised interest rates by a quarter point last week and hinted strongly it would be the last rise for some time.
But it recovered some of the lost ground on Monday.
It stood at 2.9610 marks in early afternoon trade, compared with 2.9272 marks late on Friday, still more than 20 percent higher on a trade-weighted basis than a year ago.
While subdued producer prices remove upstream price pressures from shops, analysts said other factors would conspire to drive up prices.
Steady wage growth has improved consumer confidence and the impact of extensive windfall payments from building societies converting into banks has already been felt in the shops.
"It's not producer prices that is worrying the Bank of England, it's the pace of consumer demand," said Ciaran Barr, UK economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell.
